Ash Contents in coal supplied to power sector 
†*261.      SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
   SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Coal India Limited supplies coal to the public sector 
organisations for the power generation in the country; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that the coal supplied also contains some 
quantity of ash; and 
(c) if so, the average quantity of ash therein? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRI SYED 
SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The average ash content of coal supplied for power generation is about 40%. 
Payment of Arrears to Workers of Closed Textile Mills In U.P. 
†*262. SHRI MOHD. AZAM KHAN: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state whether Government propose to take  any initiative to arrange payment of 
arrears to the workers of those textile mills  in Uttar Pradesh which arc lying closed 
and not likely to start functioning in future; if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): Responsibility for 
payment of arrears to the workers is of the owner/promoter of the mill; in case of 
winding up of a mill, the payment of arrears is to be made as per orders of the official 
liquidator. 
In the case of closed textile mills of National Textile Corporation (UP), and British 
India Corporation (BIC), Kanpur, Cent ral Government has paid wages upto 
December, 2000 and July, 2000

In respect of closed State PSUs and State Co-operative mills, Government of UP is

In respect of private sector mills, the responsibility for payment of arrears lies with 
the private owner. However, six private milk have been recommended for winding up

Import and Export of Coal 
*263. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite over two hundred billion tonnes 
of coal reserve in India, coal is imported into the country from 
Australia and other countries; 
(b) if so, the names of the countries with  the quantum of imports, the value in 
rupee terms and the reasons for such imports; and 
(c) the quantum and the countries to which coal is exported? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF COAL (SHRI SYED 
SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) and (b) Coal is under Open General Licence (OGL). 
At present, there is no limit on impor t of coal. Consumers are importing coal, 
particularly coking coal and superior quality of non-coking coal, on account of 
inadequate availability of such coals from indigenous sources. Import of coal is also 
resorted to because the present levels,of customs duty and railways freight structure 
make such imports cost competitive pet unit of calorific value on certain locations.

Problem of drinking water in Orissa 
*265. SHRI ANANTA SETHI: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state; 
(a) whether Government are aware of the increasing problem of drinking water in 
Orissa; and 
(b) if so, the details of the steps taken to tackle this problem?

(a) and (b) Drinking water supply being a State subject, schemes for providing drinking 
water facilities to rural habitations are implemented by the States from their own

financial assistance under the Centrally s ponsored Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programmes (ARWSP) and the Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programmes

Socio-economic development of Weavers 
*266. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) The steps taken for socio-economic development of the weavers by offering 
them working capital through banks promoting exports in the handloom sector; 
(b) whether most of the weavers are still using obsolete handlooms and are not 
aware of modern trends in fashion technology; and 
(c) if so, the action proposed to educate and help them in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): (a) to (c) The 
Central Government launched a comprehensive socioeconomic developmental scheme 
for weavers namely the Deen Dayal Hathkar gha Protsahan Yojana with effect from 
1.4.2000. It provides margin money to enable the weavers to get working capital loans 
from financial institutions and financial a ssistance to upgrade their looms. Besides, 
the scheme has a component of design input for weavers. 
Working capital loans are provided to handloom weavers by cooperative and 
commercial banks. These funds are entire ly refinanced by the National Bank for 
Agriculture and Rural Development (NAB ARD). Besides, the National SC & ST 
Finance and Development Corporation, Na tional Minority Finance and Development 
Corporation and National Backward Classe s Finance and Development Corporation 
also provide working capital loans to handloom weavers of identified communities. 
The export of handloom products is promoted through a scheme called the 
Development of Exportable Products for Marketing where financial assistance is 
extended by the Central Government for the development of exportable products. 
Handlooms employ traditional equipment, which are modernised wherever weavers 
so desire. This is achieved through a number of developmental schemes. Recently, the 
Central Government has set 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2001] 
up a Centre for Textile Designing where colours, design and fabric trends and 
forecasts are provided through the internet. Weavers are also covered by designers, 
who provide them with the latest designs and trends for production of better and more 
marketable fabrics and products. Weavers Service Centres and State Design Centres 
provide training to weavers in different as pects of the production of fabrics and they 
also impart awareness programmes for the upgradation of their knowledge and skills.

CAG Rips the covers off Rot in Ordnance Depot 
*272. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Wi ll the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been  drawn to the newsitem appearing in 
the Indian Express dated 6th January, 2001 , under the caption 'CAG rips the covers 
off rot in Ordnance depot'; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action proposed to be taken to prove the working of the Ordnance depots 
for better functioning? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERN ANDES): (a) to (c) The 
news-item appearing in the Indian Express is based on the Comptroller and Auditor 
General of India (CAG's) report on "Revie w of Inventory Management in Ordnace 
Services" published under reference of Uni on Government (Defence Services) No. 7-
A of 2000. This report was tabled in th e Parliament on 22.12.2000. The report of 
CAG of India was prepared after Director General of Audit Defe nce Services held 
conducted a study on this subject during 1999-2000 when its team visited five Central 
Ordnance Depots (CODs) viz; 
16 

[14 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
at Agra, Delhi Cantt., Jabalpur, Kanpur and Central Armoured Fighting Vehicle Depot 
(CAFVD) Kirkee. 
The aim of the study was to carry out a special review of the inventory management 
policies, practices and procedures, with a view to suggesting m easures to improve 
management of inventor y held by the CODs. Accordingly, a number of 
recommendations, have been made in the report, for consideration and implementation 
by the Army Ordnance Corps, in particular, as also other connected organizations like 
Department of Defence Production & Supplies, Directorate Genera] of Quality 
Assurance, Directorate of Standardization as well as the Government. 
On receipt of the CAG report, the Army Headquarters and the Army Ordnance 
Corps reviewed existing procedures and systems and took effective steps to improve the 
working of the Central Ordnance Depots. 
A deliberate and progressive approach has been adopted by the Army Headquaters 
over the years to apply modern management  techniques in the system of inventory

22.12.2000.

security agency to look after the area under its jurisdiction. A number of factors like the 
large 
44 

[14 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
tourist inflow into the Red Fort, location of a bazaar inside, holding of light and sound

local security within the perimeters of th eir own area. The incident, therefore, cannot 
be described as a reflection on the efficiency of our Defence security arrangements.

activities of terrorist groups being sponsored by certain ex ternal forces. Appropriate 
steps have been/are being taken to pre-empt such incidents in future.

Statement 
Resolutions  of the  Chief Ministers/Power Ministers Conference on 
3rd March, 2001 
I.  The Chief Ministers/Power Minister s took note of the challenges confronting 
the Power Sector. It was agreed that ther e is urgent need to depoliticise power 
sector reforms and speed up their implem entation. For this purpose, an all-party 
consensus needs to be created. The Prime Minister is requested to convene all-
party meetings including leaders of opposition in State Assemblies. 
110 

[14 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
II. The following Resolutions were adopted: 
A. COMPLETING   ELECTRIFICATION   OF   ALL   VILLAGES 
AND HOUSEHOLDS 
(i) Rural Electrification may be treate d as a Basic Minimum Service under the 
Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana; 
(ii) Rural Electrification may be completed by the end of the 10th Plan i.e. by 
year 2007; 
(iii) Full coverage of all household may be targeted for the end of the 11th Plan 
i.e. by year 2012. 
(iv) For the attainment of full electrification, States may be given flexibility for 
using funds under Rural Development Programs with the consent of the 
Village/Block Panchayats for undertaking the task of electrification where it 
is required. 
(v) It was agreed that electrification of remote villages in the States would need a 
special mode of financing including an clement of grant. 
B. DISTRIBUTION REFORMS 
The real problem of management and the challenge of reforms lies in the 
distribution sector. 
(i) Energy audit at all 11 KV feeders must be made effective within the next 6 
months and accountability fixed at the local level. 
(ii) An effective Management Informati on System for this purpose needs to be 
made operational. 
(iii) On the basis of the above, an eff ective program needs to be launched for 
identifying and eliminating power thefts in the next 2 years. 
(iv) Full metering of all consumers had been targeted for completion by December 
2001, Special efforts should be made to complete the programme. 
(v) The quality of power supplied especially  in rural areas needs to be improved 
through the APDP and other programmes quickly. 
 
 
 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2001] 
(vi) Commercial viability has to be achieved in distribution in 2-3 years through any 
or all of the following: 
—  Creating Profit centres with full accountability 
—  Handing over of local distribut ion to Panchayats/Local 
Bodics/Franchisecs/Users Associations, wherever 
necessary. 
—  Privatisation of distribution. 
—  Or any other means. 
(vii) Efforts by States, if necessary, at inviting private investment in the power sector 
need to be focussed towards the distribution sector. 
(viii) Current operations on distribution would need to reach break even in two years 
and achieve positive returns thereafter. 
C. TARIFF DETERMINATION BY REGULATORY 
COMMISSIONS AND SUBSIDIES 
(i) State Electricity Regulator y Commissions may be made functional in the next six 
months and tariff filings made. Tariff orders issued by Central Eelctricity 
Regulatory Commission and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions need to 
be implemented fully unless stayed or set aside by Court order. It is necessary to 
move away from the regime of providing free power. 
(ii) Subsidies may be given only to the extent of State Government's capacity to pay 
the subsidies explicitly through budget provisions. 
(iii) The past decision of CMs of a minimum agricultural tariff of 50 paise may be 
implemented immediately. 
D. GENERATION 
(i) Special efforts need to be made to in crease the PLF of existing plants through 
Renovation and Modernisation. 
(ii) In the short run, there is no alternative to increase in Public sector investment 
in generation, as large-scale private i nvestment in generation would flow only 
after reforms succeed in restoring financial viability. The Centre and the States 
need 
112 

[14 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
to take suitable decisions regarding increase in outlays for the 10th Plan. 
Priority should be given for investment s at those locations which produce the 
cheapest power specially for hydro projects and pit head thermal generation. 
CEA has estimated the requirement for an additional 100,000 MW of 
generating capacity by 2012. 
(iii) Where the States and Financial Institutions are in agreement about the need 
for development of IPPs, they need to  work together to achieve financial 
closure at the earliest. The Centre would facilitate the finalisation of reforms 
based multi-partite agreements. 
(iv) The evolution of a National Grid for inter-regional transfer of power needs to 
be taken up on priority. 
(v) Some provisions of the Forest Conservation Act may require to be revised for 
expeditious completion of power and other proejcts. 
E. ENERGY      CONSERVATION      AND      DEMAND      SIDE 
MANAGEMENT 
An effective program in the field of demand side management through energy 
efficient bulbs, rube lights and agricultural pumpsets, — time of the day metering and 
differential tariff for peak and off peak hours 
needs to be implemented with suitable mass awareness and extension efforts. 
F. SUPPORT FROM GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
(i) The Government of India would support the States in their reform efforts. 
This support would be linked to time bound power reform initiatives in the 
States and achievement of definite milestones towards restoration of 
financial viability. 
(ii) Interest rates of PFC and REC s hould be brought down to reflect market 
conditions. 
(iii) An Expect Group would be set up to recommend one time settlement of all 
power sector past dues to CPSUs and dues 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2001] 
from CPSUs to State Power Utilities. This would be linked to implementation 
of reforms with time bound milestones. The Group will give its report within 
three weeks of its constitution. 
G. SUPPLY FROM CENTRAL GENERATING STATIONS 
Continued supply of power from Central Ge nerating Stations would have to be 
linked to demonstration of capacity to ma ke payments for current purchases and 
securitisation of past dues. 
H. HIGH LEVEL EMPOWERED GROUP 
A High Level Empowered Group comprising of Minister of Power and Chief 
Ministers of some States may be set up to coordinate, monitor and review the 
implementation of Reforms.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (d) The Pl anning Commission in their Mid-term 
Appraisal document for the 9th Plan have  highlighted some important issues 
concerning the power sector. They are as follows: 
(i)  There is an urgent need to impr ove the financial viab ility of the State 
Electricity Boards; 
(ii)   Though reforms have been taken up in a few states, the general progress 
has been slow; 
(iii)  The success of reforms and also reduction in transmission and distribution

(iv)  The present level of transmission and distribution losses is a matter of

promoted and a specific policy should be brought out by the Government; 
(vi)   Tax concessions, as available to generating entities, should be extended to

means for obtaining additional pe aking power leading to better 
management of the system;

(x)  A Task force may be set up to analyze/examine issues related to the 
performance of the power sector dur ing 9th Plan and suggest advance 
action for the 10th Plan etc. 
The Government is seized of the issues  which have been highlighted by the 
Planning Commission. Reforms in the power sector is a thrust area and the 
Government has enacted the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998 which has 
paved the way for the setting up of Centra l Electricity Regulatory Commission which 
would, in due course, rationalize tariffs . Fifteen State Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions have so far been set up in as  many States. The Government has also 
initiated a new scheme by the name Accelerated Power Development Programme 
(APDP) with a budgetary outlay of Rs. 1000 crore for this financial year from which 
assistance would be given to the States for not only renovation and modernisation but 
also for strengthening of their transmission and distribution systems. On the subject of 
rural electrification, the Finance Minister in his Budget Speech on 28.2.2001 has 
announced inter-alia that rural electrification will henceforth be one of the components 
which would be considered under the Prime Minister's Gramodya Yojana. Separately, 
the Government has also asked a Group of Ministers to give their recommendations on 
various issues concerning rural electrification including how to enhance the pace of 
electrification. The issues highlighted by the Planning Commission are discussed with 
the States periodically and the last su ch discussion took place during the Chief 
Ministers/Power Ministers Conference he ld on 3.3.2001 at New Delhi, which had a 
focus on power sector reforms. This conference adopted a number of landmark 
resolutions to improve the financial health and operational efficien cy of power sector 
utilities and accelerate the pace of reforms.

Statement 
Details of Schemes being implemented for the benefit of handloom 
weavers 
A. Development of Exportable Products and their marketing Scheme: 
This scheme aims at giving substantial im petus to the export of handloom fabrics, 
made-ups and other handloom items from the country. 
B. Mill Gate Price Scheme: 
In order to ensure the adequate supply of yarn to weavers, all types of yarn required 
for the production of handloom items are supplied at prices prevailing at the Mill Gate 
Price i.e. without any added transportation cost, by the National Handloom 
Development Corporation. 
C. Marketing  through  National  Handloom  Expos,  Districts  Level 
Events, Fairs, Melas etc. 
These events are organised to enable the handloom weavers to learn market trends, 
design development, the taste of the customer and also to market their products. 
D. Decentralised Training of Weavers: 
The objective of the scheme is to bring about skill up-gradation in the skilled and 
semi-skilled category of handloom weavers for enhancing their earning capacity, 
simultaneously ensuring development of marketable products. 
E. Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana 
With a view to improve the infrastructure facility fo r product diversification and 
quality upgradation as well as to  support the efforts of marketing, design, consultancy 
etc., a comprehensive scheme Deendayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana has been 
introduced w.e.f. 1.4.2000. 
The objective of the scheme is:— 
To provide necessary support for product diversification, quality up-gradation,  
strengthen   the   handloom  organizations  to  provide 
201 

RAJYA SABHA         [14 March, 2001] 
inputs to the weavers, ensure availability of infrastructure and common fac ilities better 
products and marketing avenues, improve mobility of finished handloom products from the 
State of J&K and North Eastern States including Sikkim, provide suitable marketing 
incentives to attract buyers towards handloom goods. 
2. Apart from the above, for taking care of the well being of the handloom weavers the 
Government of India is also implementing certain schemes exclusively for the welfare of 
the weavers. These are as follows:— 
F. Workshed-cum-Housing Scheme: 
This Scheme was introduced with the objective of providing a dwelling unit and suitable 
work place to weavers to improve their productivity, quality of life and earnings. The 
assistance under the scheme is Rs. 7000/- for Rural Workshed and Rs. 10,000/- for Urban 
Workshed. The assistance is Rs, 18,000/- for rural Workshed-cum-Houses and Rs. 20,000/- 
for Urban Workshed-cum-Houses. 
G. Thrift Fund Scheme: 
The Scheme envisages the creation of a type of provident fund with contribution from the 
weavers, for facilitating them to meet expenses towards children's education/medical 
expenses of family members and expenses in c onnection with marriage and other 
religious ceremonies. The weavers contribute 8% of the wages and the Central and State 
Governments contribute 4% each. 
H. Health Package Scheme: 
This scheme extends financial assistance to weavers for the treatment of diseases like, 
asthama, TB, inflammation of respiratory system, cost of testing of eyes and spectacles, 
supply of drinking water, maternity benefits to women weavers, payment of add itional 
compensation of adopting permanent family planning measures and infrastructure for primary 
health care. 
202 

[14 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
I. Group Insurance Scheme: 
Group Insurance Scheme was introduced in order to meet the Socio-economic obligation of 
weavers towards his family and the uncertainty of his working capacity in old age. Under the 
scheme a weaver is provided an insurance coverage of Rs. 10,000/- for an annual 
premium of Rs. 120/-. The premium is shared equally among the beneficiary, State and 
Central Governments. 
J. New Insurance Scheme for Handloom Weavers: 
In order to provide relief to handloom weavers, a New Insurance Scheme for Handloom 
Weavers is being implemented through United India Insurance Company. The scheme provides 
coverage of various types of risks such as loss of life, limbs, eyes in the event of accident. 
Under the scheme, there is a coverage in respect of damage of dwelling unit and the raw 
material in the case of natural calamities. The premium is Rs. 120/- with a contribution of 
Rs. 20/- by the weaver, Rs. 40/-by State Government and Rs. 60/- by the Government of 
India.
